question: Where was the Roman glass from the Silla royal tomb made?
answer: The sources retrieved do not answer this question. The only source specifically about the Silla royal tomb glass, S1, supplies solely the object's designation as "경주 98호 남분 유리병 및 잔 (慶州 九十八號 南墳 琉璃甁 및 盞) — Glass Ewer and Cups from the South Mound of Tomb No. 98, Gyeongju" and its National Treasure listing, with no statement in its source text about where the glass was manufactured [S1]; the remaining sources concern Roman-linked finds and contacts in Southeast Asia, South Asia, Scandinavia, and Chinese textual records of an embassy, none of which address the origin of the Gyeongju glassware [S2][S3][S4][S5][S6].

english.text: 경주 98호 남분 유리병 및 잔 (慶州 九十八號 南墳 琉璃甁 및 盞) — Glass Ewer and Cups from the South Mound of Tomb No. 98, Gyeongju. Designated National Treasure No. 193, 7 December 1978.

The remains found at Oc Eo include pottery, tools, jewelry, casts for making jewelry, coins, and religious statues. Among the finds are gold jewellery imitating coins from the Roman Empire of the Antonine period... Oc Eo was near Chinese-controlled Jiaozhou and the region where Chinese historical texts claim the Romans first landed before venturing further into China to conduct diplomacy in 166.
Signature on the silver cups: [ΧEIPI]ΣΟΦΟΣ ЄΠΟΙΕΙ ('Cheirisophos made [this]'); engraved owner's name: SILIVS.

Mediterranean objects (100 BC to 400 AD): Amphora and terra sigillata shards; fragments of Roman glass pillar bowls; and gaming counters. West Asian, South Arabian, and Mesopotamian objects (300 BC to 1000 AD): turquoise glazed pottery; torpedo jar fragments; frankincense crumbs. Most remarkable: a fired brick wharf complex with nine teak bollards and a mummified 6-metre dugout canoe (Artocarpus hirsutus).

In the ninth yanxi year [166 CE], during the reign of Emperor Huan, the king of Da Qin (the Roman Empire), Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus), sent envoys from beyond the frontiers through Rinan (Commandery on the central Vietnamese coast), to offer elephant tusks, rhinoceros horn, and turtle shell. This was the very first time there was [direct] communication [between the two countries]. The tribute brought was neither precious nor rare, raising suspicion that the accounts [of the 'envoys'] might be exaggerated.
english.attribution: John E. Hill, '"Chapter on the Western Regions" from Hou Hanshu 88', draft annotated translation, University of Washington Silk Road Seattle project.

english.text: Gudme III: a hoard of 293 Roman silver coins (siliquae) from the 4th century AD. A related treasure included nine gold bracteates, a small sword stud with garnets in cloisonne, a finger ring, two round pendants and a worn Roman silver denarius.
